info.bio:
Charles Edward Anderson Berry (18 de octubre de 1926 - 18 de marzo de 2017) nació el 18 de octubre de 1926 en St. Louis. Su madre, Martha, era profesora y su padre, Henry, contratista y diácono bautista. Es el tercero de seis hermanos. 

Es una figura influyente y uno de los pioneros del rock and roll.

Berry había estado tocando blues desde sus adolescencia y a principios de 1953, comienza a ganarse un sobresueldo tocando en la "Sir John's Trio" una banda que actuaba en un popular club de Saint Louis.

scenes.name: Soul y R&B
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 1 de enero de 1966 el Top 3 estadounidense lo formaban «The Sound of Silence», «We Can Work It Out» y el «I Got You (I Feel Good)» de James Brown: discos futuristas los tres. A finales de mes Otis Redding se acercaba al Top 10 británico con su versión de «My Girl» de los Temptations.

scenes.name: Rhythm and blues
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: En los cuarenta, los combos de jump como el Tympany Five de Louis Jordan sustituyeron a las big bands: baile, ritmo, scat, solo de saxo. Gente que trabajaba duro todo el día necesitaba música fuerte y con alma: un grito sincero, un saxo, una guitarra rockera. Su «misma vulgaridad», dice LeRoi Jones, aseguraba su conexión con la vida de la gente, y esa vulgaridad fue el ingrediente principal del funk. Despreciado por los intelectuales como mal jazz, el R&B dio a Chuck Berry, Little Richard y Bo Diddley, inspiró el rock and roll y la invasión británica, y en el chitlin circuit fue el útero del funk. Con Live at the Apollo de James Brown (1962, disco de oro) el R&B se hizo mayor; de él salieron Ray Charles, Brown y Aretha Franklin.
scenes.family: Raíces: blues, jazz, gospel y R&B

scenes.name: Contracultura, Sgt. Pepper y Woodstock
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La revolución negra sacudió también a la juventud blanca: la cuestión moral de los derechos civiles, el racismo familiar, la atracción por la cultura negra, el miedo al reclutamiento y las drogas. Dylan y los Beatles convirtieron el rock en forma de vida. Sgt. Pepper (1967), de unos Beatles criados con Chuck Berry («a mí no me ha pasado nada desde 1958, cuando oí el rock and roll negro», dijo Lennon), abrió la era psicodélica que influiría en Electric Ladyland de Hendrix y en el Free Your Mind… de Funkadelic; Sly salió en el Ed Sullivan con uniforme de banda, y de ahí viene el púrpura de Prince. La contracultura sintetizó jazz, R&B, pop, rock y folk en formas largas, espectáculos de luces y tecnología, rasgos que el black rock (Hendrix, Sly, Funkadelic, War, Ohio Players, los Isley, Bar-Kays) llevó al funk. En Woodstock (1969) brillaron Hendrix, Sly y Santana. Las muertes de Hendrix, Joplin y Morrison, Altamont, Kent State y Jackson State acabaron con la idea de que el rock cambiaría el mundo; en la música negra el funk mantuvo vivos esos ideales.
scenes.family: Funk psicodélico y black rock: Sly, Hendrix

scenes.name: Hard rock americano: Aerosmith, Kiss y Alice Cooper
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: En Estados Unidos la crítica, que detesta a Black Sabbath y a Judas Priest, evita el término «heavy metal» y prefiere «hard rock», el formato radiofónico de moda en los setenta, donde caben grupos muy populares que no cumplen del todo el código: Aerosmith (1973) y Kiss (1974) son demasiado melódicos para ser heavy en esa década. Cuando el género se fragmente, el lite metal adoptará su estilo vocal melódico y sus armonías, y ambos acabarán dentro del metal ampliado. Alice Cooper, que compartía cartel con Black Sabbath, regala al heavy la estética visual de película de terror.
scenes.family: Raíces: blues rock, psicodelia y hard rock

scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

scenes.name: Detroit: MC5 y Stooges
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La ciudad más industrial de EE UU y cuartel de los elementos más extremistas de la contracultura: un rock'n'roll feroz y ruidoso se convierte en la voz de los obreros y de sus hijos. Los MC5 de John Sinclair, ala revolucionaria de las revueltas estudiantiles (Kick Out The Jams, «el equivalente rockero de una explosión nuclear»); los Stooges de Iggy Pop, síntesis de Chuck Berry, Rolling Stones, Velvet Underground y Doors que inventa el punk-rock («1970») y el voodoobilly («TV Eye»). Un nuevo rock'n'roll fundado en la violencia extrema.
scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

podcast.title: Explosion into Public Consciousness (1955)
podcast.body: Chuck Berry, along with Elvis, Little Richard, Bo Diddly, and Bill Haley, exploded into public consciousness in 1955, marking the birth of rock and roll. "they all exploded into public consciousness that year, 1955, the birth of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sustained Rock and Roll Success (1956)
podcast.body: Chuck Berry was recognized as one of the key black R&B stars who continued to achieve significant rock and roll hits on the charts by late 1956, during a period when many white rockabilly acts were declining. "If we're talking about actual rock and roll hits rising to decent positions in the charts, by late 1956 you're looking at acts like Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Fat Stomano with only Elvis left of the rock-a-billy's."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "Go Johnny Go" Film Appearance (1959)
podcast.body: Chuck Berry co-starred as himself with Alan Fried in the 1959 film "Go Johnny Go," which took its title from Berry's hit song. The movie proved to be a final moment of rock and roll cultural relevance for many involved, as several featured artists faced professional decline or untimely deaths shortly after its release. "That film came out in 1959 and had Barry as Fried's co-star, appearing with Fried as himself in almost every scene."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Post-Prison Commercial Resurgence (1964)
podcast.body: Serving 18 months in jail unexpectedly revitalized Chuck Berry's commercial prospects. Upon his release in 1964, his first three singles—"Nadine," "You Never Can Tell," and "No Particular Place To Go"—were all bigger hits than he had experienced since 1958, suggesting a potential return to the top. "As odd as it is to say, Barry's 18 months in jail may have done him some good as a commercial prospect."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Studio Work Decline After 1964
podcast.body: Following a brief commercial resurgence in 1964, Chuck Berry's studio recordings largely reverted to mediocrity, marked by only occasional flashes of his earlier brilliance. This period saw a general decline in the quality of his new music. "But it was a false dawn. Barry's studio works slid back into mediocrity with occasional flashes of his old brilliance."

podcast.title: Connection to "Good Avenue" in "Johnny B. Good"
podcast.body: The title "Johnny B. Good" subtly refers to Chuck Berry's childhood home, which was located at 2520 Good Avenue. The spelling of "Goode" in the song's title, with an 'E' at the end, mirrors the street name, linking the narrative to Berry's personal history. "Barry is spelled G-O-O-D-E with an E on the end, and Barry's childhood home was at 2520 Good Avenue with an E."

podcast.title: Defining Rock's Style and Persona
podcast.body: Berry created much of the standard rock and roll style, characterized by his two and three-chord electric guitar riffs, swagger, and attitude. His lyrics specifically targeted youth culture, exploring themes of adolescent trouble, and his emphasis on guitar solos was central to his sound, foreshadowing later developments in rock despite predating advanced amplification and distortion. "More than any other person, he made rock into a separate and distinct thing, riffing through two and three chord songs on his electric guitar with style and showmanship."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disputes on the Alan Freed Tour
podcast.body: Chuck Berry was a key figure in the legendary Alan Freed tour, known more for the personal disputes between him and Jerry Lee Lewis than for the music. One conflict involved Lewis's father, Elmo, who, following a parking dispute between Berry and Lewis, chased Berry with a knife, shouting racial slurs and threats, though the two were friendly by the next day. Berry also believed he should be headlining the shows over Lewis and managed to persuade promoters of this, leading Lewis to attempt increasingly outrageous onstage stunts to upstage him. "The tour later became legendary, not so much for the music, though that was great, but for the personal disputes between Lewis and Berry."

podcast.title: Father of Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Chuck Berry is widely recognized as the "father of rock and roll" for his pivotal role in transforming rhythm and blues into a distinct genre. More than any other artist, he defined the standard rock and roll style with his electric guitar riffs, showmanship, and lyrics aimed at young people, laying the foundation for much of what followed. "If anyone can be credited with being the first to take rhythm and blues and rocking it up, it's got to be him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Generation Guitar Hero
podcast.body: Chuck Berry is listed among the first to be declared a "guitar hero," recognized for his seemingly supernatural mastery of the electric guitar. "We had Chuck Berry... They were among the first to be declared guitar heroes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundational Rock Duo
podcast.body: Chuck Berry, along with Elvis Presley, is recognized for delivering the initial impact that set rock music on its course. "Not one two-punch of Elvis and Chuck started us on the road to where we are today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Guitar Intro Innovation for "Johnny B. Good"
podcast.body: While the basic riff for the intro to "Johnny B. Good" was derived from earlier blues and jazz records, such as Carl Hogan's playing on Louis Jordan's "Ain't That Just Like A Woman," Chuck Berry made a crucial innovation. He played the solo line on two strings instead of one, creating a thicker sound with parallel harmonies, a technique he learned from T-Bone Walker. This subtle change transmuted a common musical phrase into a signature part instantly identifiable with him. "The crucial change Barry makes there is that most of the time he's playing the solo line on two strings instead of one, creating a thicker sound with parallel harmonies, rather than just the simple melody line."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Imprisonment for Transporting a Minor
podcast.body: Chuck Berry served five years in prison after being convicted of transporting a 14-year-old girl across state lines for "immoral purposes." This conviction significantly impacted his early career. "Chuck Berry, five years in prison for transporting a 14-year-old girl across state lines for immoral purposes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inconsistent Chart Performance Before Arrest
podcast.body: Chuck Berry's career trajectory was not a continuous upward curve; after his breakout hit "School Day," his next single "Oh Baby Doll" was a comparative flop. Even before his arrest in 1959, his singles had an inconsistent chart history, with only five of his first eleven singles making the top 10 on the pop charts, and classics like "30 Days" and "Brown-Eyed Handsome Man" failing to chart at all. "Barry's career didn't go on a completely upward curve after that point. His next single, Oh Baby Doll, was a comparative flop."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.title: Influence from Charlie Christian
podcast.body: Chuck Berry later stated that Charlie Christian was one of the biggest influences on his guitar playing, despite wrongly associating Christian with Tommy Dorsey's band instead of Benny Goodman's. This acknowledgment underlines Christian's significant, though sometimes misattributed, impact on early rock and roll guitarists. "Chuck Berry later said the Christian was one of the biggest influences on his guitar playing, though he wrongly said the Christian played with Tommy Dorses band, arrival to Goodman's."

podcast.body: Chuck Berry is mentioned as a specific influence on U2, particularly regarding the "first electric guitars," contributing to U2's exploration of classic American music roots. "incluso de las primeras guitarras eléctricas en Chuck Berry."

podcast.title: Inspired by Louis Jordan
podcast.body: Chuck Berry was one of the artists who drew inspiration from Louis Jordan, who led the most popular R&B group in the late 1940s and early 1950s. "The one that inspired everyone from Chuck Berry to Bill Haley."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Interstellar Ambassador of Rock
podcast.body: In 1977, one rock and roll song by Chuck Berry was included on the Voyager Golden Disk, a gold phonograph record attached to the Voyager I and Voyager II spacecraft. This means that if an advanced alien species ever discovers these probes, their very first introduction to rock music will come from a Black man, enduring for infinity. "And if an alien civilization ever finds one of our Voyager probes, their introduction, their first exposure to rock will come from a black man."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jerry Lee Lewis's Piano Style Influence
podcast.body: The popularity of Jerry Lee Lewis and his "ripping" piano technique, where fingers slide across keys quickly, significantly influenced the piano style on Chuck Berry's records. Leonard Chess insisted on Berry's regular player, Johnny Johnson, adopting this technique for new recordings despite Johnson's initial dislike for it. "This is because of the popularity of Jerry Lee Lewis, who had risen to fame since Berry's last session. Lewis tended to use a simple technique called ripping when playing the piano."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: John Lennon's Rock and Roll Epithet
podcast.body: John Lennon famously stated, "if you tried to give rock and roll another name, it would be Chook Barry." This quote underscores Berry's foundational and indispensable role in shaping the genre, for both its positive and negative aspects. "John Lennon once said, if you tried to give rock and roll another name, it would be Chook Barry, and for both better and worse, that's probably true."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Johnny B. Goode
podcast.body: In Rick Nelson's 1972 song "Garden Party," Chuck Berry is referenced under the code name "Johnny Be Good," acknowledging his presence on the concert bill. "Nelson calls Chuck Berry Johnny Be Good, for example."

podcast.title: Later Arrest for Voyeurism
podcast.body: Years after his initial prison sentence, Chuck Berry was arrested again for videotaping women in a public restroom, indicating a pattern of problematic behavior. "He was later arrested for videotaping women in a public restroom."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Likely influenced by Nat King Cole
podcast.body: Chuck Berry's "Havana Moon" was "almost certainly inspired by Nat King Cole's 'Calypso Blues'." This highlights the chain of influence in popular music. "Of course, nothing is original, and the Chuck Barry track itself was almost certainly inspired by that King tolls, Colipso Blues."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Lyrics Origin for "Johnny B. Good"
podcast.body: Chuck Berry initially conceived the lyric for "Johnny B. Good" as a personal message to his pianist, Johnny Johnson, urging him to "stop drinking so much." However, this quickly evolved into a song about Berry himself, or an idealized version of him, which was even more explicit in the original lyric where he sang "a coloured boy" instead of "a country boy." "Barry always talked about how the original idea for the lyric was as a message to Johnny Johnson saying, Johnny Be Good, stop drinking so much."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.title: Mann Act Conviction and Racial Injustice
podcast.body: In December 1959, Chuck Berry was arrested for having sexual relations with a 14-year-old sex worker he had met in Texas and then fired from his St. Louis nightclub. He was charged and convicted under the Mann Act, also known as the White Slave Traffic Act, a law historically created to punish black men. While the prosecution was racially motivated and the judge made racist remarks, leading to a reduced sentence, Berry did serve time in prison from 1961. "Like Lewis, Barry has been more or less forgiven by the consensus narrative of rock history. There is slightly more justification for doing so in Barry's case than in Lewis's, because the man act, the law under which he was charged and convicted, was a law that was created specifically to punish black men."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Musical Preferences and Influences
podcast.body: While Chuck Berry played Louis Jordan's music to make a living, he stated that Nat King Cole was the musician he most liked to listen to, indicating a significant personal influence on his musical tastes. "Barry would often say that while Louis Jordan music was the music he would play to try to make a living, Nat King Cold was the musician he most liked to listen to..."

podcast.title: Myth of Career Wreckage by Arrest
podcast.body: The popular belief that Chuck Berry's career was completely ruined by his 1959 arrest is a myth. While "Johnny B. Good" was his last top 10 hit for several years, his chart performance had already been inconsistent, with many classics failing to chart. His decline was more attributable to shifting public tastes and the quality of his material in the late 50s and early 60s, rather than solely his legal troubles. "There's a myth that Barry's career was completely wrecked by his arrest. This simply isn't true."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.title: Reasons for Late 50s/Early 60s Chart Decline
podcast.body: Chuck Berry's reduced chart success in the late 1950s and early 1960s was due to two main factors: a natural shift in public taste, which few singles artists from the 50s could survive, and his own admission that the material he recorded after "Johnny B. Good" was not his best. Many of these later songs, such as "Anthony Boy" and "Too Pooped to Pop," are largely forgotten. "The first is that public taste had moved on as it does every few years. There are very few singles artists, and all artists in the 50s were singles artists, who can survive a major change in the public's taste."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.title: Reconciliation with Jerry Lee Lewis After Boston Incident
podcast.body: Despite prior tension and fighting throughout their 1958 co-headlining tour, the shared adversity faced during a controversial Boston concert, where police intervened, brought Chuck Berry and Jerry Lee Lewis together. Following this event, they became close friends and spoke highly of each other. "Oddly, going through this adversity seems to have brought Barry and Jerry Lee Lewis together. While they'd been fighting each other for almost the entire tour, after this point they became quite close friends and would speak only about each other."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.title: Respect from Jerry Lee Lewis
podcast.body: Despite their constant fighting, Chuck Berry was one of the few people for whom Jerry Lee Lewis showed genuine respect. Lewis greatly admired Berry's songwriting, referring to him as "the Hank Williams of Rock and Roll," which was the highest possible praise from Lewis. Furthermore, Lewis and his father were careful to conceal their feuds from Lewis's mother, who considered Chuck Berry "the greatest rock and roller in the world," even superior to Elvis and her own son, and would have sided with Berry. "But also, Lewis and his father were both always very careful not to do anything that would lead to word of the feud getting back to his mother, because his mother had repeatedly told him that Chuck Berry was the greatest rock and roller in the world."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Retirement from New Music and Touring Style
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, Chuck Berry essentially ceased making new music. For the next nearly 40 years, he toured the world exclusively with his guitar, relying on local pickup bands provided by promoters and often not informing them of the next song, confident that everyone knew his extensive repertoire. "In the late 70s, Barry essentially retired from making new music, choosing instead to spend the best part of 40 years touring the world with just his guitar, playing with whatever local pickup band the promoter could scrape together."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Rock and Roll Foundation
podcast.body: In the 1950s, a 30-year-old black man from St. Louis, Chuck Berry, was instrumental in forming the very foundation of rock and roll by laying down essential guitar riffs and an influential attitude. "a 30-year-old black man from St. Louis named Chuck Berry was laying down guitar riffs and an attitude that ended up forming the very foundation of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Similar 1950s Rock Structure
podcast.body: Chuck Berry upheld the characteristic canons of 1950s rock, much like Little Richard. His songs consistently featured a very acute guitar sound that would alternate with his vocals, allowing his acute vocal register to be clearly heard when he sang. "Chuck Berry vamos a ver que tiene una estructura muy similar y que mantiene mucho esos mismos canones."

podcast.title: Steve Martin's "Send More Chuck Berry" Joke
podcast.body: On Saturday Night Live the week the Voyager probe was launched, comedian Steve Martin famously joked about a message from aliens stating, "Send more Chuck Berry." This anecdote highlights the immense cultural significance and recognition of "Johnny Be Good" at the time. "On Saturday Night Live, the week the probe was launched, Steve Martin joked that there been a message from aliens. Send more Chuck Berry."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.title: Touring Practice – Cash Payment Requirement
podcast.body: In the days before he encountered tax troubles with the IRS and adopted more conventional bookkeeping, Chuck Berry famously demanded his performance fee to be delivered in cash, in a paper bag, before the show. If the bag full of money was not present, the gig would not happen. "His performance fee had to be delivered in cash in a paper bag before the show, and if there was no bag full of money, there was no gig."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring Practice – Local Backing Band Requirements
podcast.body: For his performances, Chuck Berry required the local backup band to be familiar with all his songs and to consist of a drummer, a pianist, and one bass player. They needed to be available for at least three hours prior to showtime for rehearsal, even though Chuck himself often showed up only five minutes before the lights went down. "The local band had to be familiar with all of Chuck's songs, and must include a drummer, a pianist, and one bass player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring Practice – No Permanent Band
podcast.body: Chuck Berry, known as the father of rock and roll, did not tour with a fixed backing band due to the expense. Instead, he expected promoters to easily find a local backup band for him, as "everybody in the world knew his songs." "he did not tour with a band, it's too expensive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring Practice – Specific Equipment and Luxury Transport
podcast.body: Chuck Berry traveled only with his guitar and demanded a very specific Fender amp to be supplied. Additionally, he required a brand new rented Mercedes S-Class vehicle, and only an S-Class, for the duration of his visit to the city, with all gas, insurance, and mileage paid. "Chuck traveled only with his guitar. He also needed to be supplied with a very specific fender amp."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Voyager Probes' Golden Record Inclusion
podcast.body: Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Good" was the sole rock and roll song selected for inclusion on the golden record sent into space aboard NASA's Voyager probes in the 1970s. The selection, which also featured classical pieces, world music, and greetings, was initially criticized for containing any rock and roll, but the record is now the furthest human-made object from Earth. "Johnny Be Good is so much the epitome of American post-war culture that when NASA sent a record into space on the Voyager probes in the 70s, it was the only rock and roll song included in the selection of audio."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: Godmother of Rock and Roll
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, a queer Black woman from Cotton Plant, Arkansas, is widely called the "Godmother of rock and roll." She was a pioneering guitarist who transitioned to the electric guitar, revered by figures like Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis, Elvis Presley, Little Richard, and Chuck Berry for her influential bridge between gospel blues and swing music. "A lot of people will point to sister Rosetta Thar, a guitarist who graduated to the electric guitar and has been called the Godmother of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Profound Influence on Blues and Rock Pioneers
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe had a deep impact on the trajectory of the blues and on the pioneers of rock and roll, including major figures like Little Richard, Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Johnny Cash, all of whom were ardent fans. Her work also captivated British musicians such as Keith Richards, Eric Clapton, and Jeff Beck. "What is not in dispute is that sister Rosetta Tharp had a profound effect on the course of the blues, and then with the pioneers of rock."
